newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: War on inflation crucial - S.African Reserve Bank.
newsitem.headline: War on inflation crucial - S.African Reserve Bank.

text.p: The reintegration of South Africa into international financial markets had made it crucial to apply consistent policies to reduce inflation, Reserve Bank economic adviser Ernie van der Merwe said on Monday.
Addressing the Commonwealth Press Union's biennial conference, Van der Merwe said that it was "even more essential (now) for the monetary authorities to achieve the objective of price stability.

"The pursuit of price stability in the rest of the world and the success achieved by many countries in this regard has left South Africa with really no other alternative but to keep its rate of inflation in step with that of the rest of the world."
This would ensure South Africa's competitiveness and allow for high and sustainable economic growth, he said.
He said South Africa had been able to reduce inflation from a peak of 18.6 percent in 1986 to 7.5 percent in August this year.

"Despite this slowdown in the rate of increase of consumer prices, there still exists an inflation differential of about five percent between South Africa and its major trading partners. For the attainment of general financial stability, it is crucial that this differential be eliminated," he said.
Achieving this was being made difficult by volatile cross-border capital movements.

"Such a policy does however not provide unconditional protection against sudden capital movements, giving rise to the so-called confidence gap. As a result there may be pressures to counteract internal imbalances of monetary policy measures. "Such an approach appears to be extremely risky because in the end monetary policy may concentrate too much on countering speculative capital flows instead of the more important objective of price stability."
Van der Merwe said one of the challenges facing South Africa was reducing its dependence on foreign capital inflows while increasing domestic savings ratios.

"One of the most disconcerting developments in South Africa has been the continued decrease in the ratio of domestic savings to gross domestic product from a level of about 25 percent in the middle of the 1980s to just about 16 percent in the first half of 1996," he said.
This poor savings performance was mainly due to the high propensity of South African households to consume.
"The recent efforts of the government to reduce the fiscal deficit... must therefore be applauded," he said.

The sharp volatility in capital movements over the last few years also indicated how important it was that South Africa "attracted the right kind of capital, that is direct investment rather than portfolio and short term capital," he said.
He therefore welcomed moves to make South Africa a more investor friendly country "which hopefully should attract more permanent and longer term capital".
